passages.t: ‘Everyone in the entire congregation is holy’
passages.happening:
Korah, a Levite of the clan of Kohath, rises against Moses. With him are Dathan and Abiram of the tribe of Reuben, and 250 well-known leaders (verses 1-2).

They say to Moses and Aaron, “You have taken too much upon yourselves! For everyone in the entire congregation is holy, and the LORD is in their midst. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?” (verse 3).

Moses falls facedown. Then he sets a test. Tomorrow Korah and his followers are to bring censers with fire and incense before the LORD. “Then the man the LORD chooses will be the one who is holy” (verse 7). He says to the Levites, ‘He has brought you near, you and all your fellow Levites, but you are seeking the priesthood as well’ (verse 10).

Moses sends for Dathan and Abiram. They refuse: “We will not come!” (verse 12). They accuse him of bringing them ‘out of a land flowing with milk and honey to kill us in the wilderness’ and of making himself ruler (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
After Kadesh the crisis turns inward. The question is no longer whether Israel will trust God for the land. It is who has the right to lead, and who may come near to God for the people.

The chapter weaves together two complaints. Korah and the 250 challenge Aaron's priesthood. Dathan and Abiram challenge Moses' leadership. Many critical scholars think two older stories have been joined. Others read one account of an alliance with mixed motives. Either way the text keeps both threads.

The people are placed with care. Korah belongs to the Kohathites, the clan that carried the ark and the holiest furniture (chapter 4). He was already nearer to holy things than almost anyone. Dathan and Abiram are from Reuben, the tribe of Jacob's firstborn, which might have expected a leading place and never received it. Kohathites and Reubenites camped on the same side of the tabernacle, the south, which may be how the alliance formed.

Korah's words are partly true, and that is what makes them strong. All Israel was called to be holy. God did live among them. A reader should feel the pull of the argument. It sounds like a plea for the whole people against leaders who have set themselves up.

Moses answers that he and Aaron did not set themselves up. God chose them, and God can say so. And he names what lies under the fine words. Korah already has a great gift, and it is not enough for him. The complaint that the leaders take too much comes from a man who wants more.

Dathan and Abiram say something worse. They call Egypt ‘a land flowing with milk and honey’. That is God's phrase for Canaan. They have taken the name of the promise and given it to the house of slavery. And they blame Moses for the failure at Kadesh, which was the people's own.

The same phrases pass back and forth. ‘You have taken too much upon yourselves’, say the rebels, and Moses says it back to them (verse 7). ‘Is it not enough’ comes on both sides (verses 9, 13). The Hebrew word for ‘congregation’ comes nineteen times in the chapter. The whole quarrel is about who speaks for it.
passages.later:
Psalm 106 remembers the day: “In the camp they envied Moses, as well as Aaron, the holy one of the LORD” (Psalm 106:16).

Hebrews says of the high priesthood, “No one takes this honor upon himself; he must be called by God, just as Aaron was” (Hebrews 5:4). And it adds that Christ too ‘did not take upon Himself the glory of becoming a high priest’ (Hebrews 5:5).

Paul echoes Moses' words in verse 5, that God will show who belongs to him: “The Lord knows those who are His” (2 Timothy 2:19).
passages.hard:
Was Korah not right? The Bible itself says that all God's people are holy.

It does. God had said at Sinai that Israel would be ‘a kingdom of priests and a holy nation’ (Exodus 19:6). Moses himself wished that all the LORD's people were prophets (11:29). The New Testament calls the whole church ‘a royal priesthood’ (1 Peter 2:9).

The story does not condemn that truth. It condemns the use Korah made of it. He was not asking for the people to be lifted up. He was reaching for an office God had given to someone else, and Moses says so in verse 10. In the same book, the same Moses is glad when God's Spirit rests on others without his leave.

This chapter has often been misused. Leaders have called anyone who questioned them a Korah. The text gives no support to that. Moses and Aaron were appointed by God in a way no pastor or leader today can claim, and even so Moses could say, ‘I have not taken one donkey from them or mistreated a single one of them’ (verse 15). The rest of Scripture expects leaders to be questioned, tested and corrected. The prophets rebuked kings and priests. Paul opposed Peter to his face (Galatians 2:11).

And nothing in this passage shields a leader who does harm. Christians agree that leaders are servants accountable to Christ and to his word, and that no authority may be used to cover abuse. If a leader uses his place to control, exploit or harm, these verses do not protect him. Anyone harmed by a church leader is free to speak to another trusted leader, a counselor, or, where a crime is involved, the authorities. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Korah had been given a place near the holy things, and he looked at what he had not been given. Ask what good gift of your own you have stopped seeing because you are watching someone else's. And ask whether your complaints about those who lead you are for the good of the people, or for yourself.

passages.happening:
The next morning each man stands with his censer at the entrance to the tent. Korah gathers the whole assembly against Moses and Aaron, and the glory of the LORD appears (verses 18-19).

God says to Moses and Aaron, “Separate yourselves from this congregation so that I may consume them in an instant” (verse 21). “But Moses and Aaron fell facedown and said, ‘O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, when one man sins, will You be angry with the whole congregation?’” (verse 22).

God tells the people to move away from the tents of Korah, Dathan and Abiram, and they do (verses 24-27). Dathan and Abiram stand at their tent doors with their wives, children and infants.

Moses says that if these men die an ordinary death, the LORD has not sent him. “As soon as Moses had finished saying all this, the ground beneath them split open, and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them and their households” (verses 31-32). “And fire came forth from the LORD and consumed the 250 men who were offering the incense” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
The test Moses set was pointed. Offering incense before God was a priest's work. Leviticus had told how two of Aaron's own sons died for bringing fire God had not commanded (Leviticus 10:1-2). If the 250 claim the standing of priests, they are to do what priests do, and God will show whom he accepts.

For the third time in the book God speaks of ending the whole people, and again Moses and Aaron fall on their faces and plead. Their prayer asks whether everyone should suffer for one man's sin. God answers by drawing a line. The people are warned and told to step away. The judgment falls on the tents of the leaders of the revolt, after everyone has had the chance to leave them.

Sheol is the Old Testament's usual name for the place of the dead, pictured as lying under the earth. In most passages it is simply where all the dead go. It is not, in itself, a place of punishment. What makes this event terrible is that the rebels go down alive, all at once, with all they own. The text says nothing about what they met there.

These are among the most frightening verses in Numbers, and the fear of the people in verse 34 is the natural response. A reader is not asked to enjoy them. The story presents the event as ‘something unprecedented’ (verse 30), a sign given once to settle a question on which the life of the whole camp depended.
passages.later:
The law of Moses forbids a human court to punish children for their parents' crimes: “Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin” (Deuteronomy 24:16).

Numbers itself adds a line that changes how the story is heard: “However, the line of Korah did not die out” (26:11). Later a group of psalms is headed as belonging to the sons of Korah. One of them says, “I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of the wicked” (Psalm 84:10).

Jude names ‘Korah’s rebellion’ as a warning about teachers who serve themselves (Jude 1:11).
passages.hard:
Why were the wives, children and infants of Dathan and Abiram swallowed with them?

This is one of the hardest pictures in the book, and it should not be explained away.

Readers have pointed to several things. In the ancient world a household was seen as one body that stood or fell with its head. The whole congregation was warned to move away from these tents, and the families stayed where they were (verses 24-27). Neither point makes the death of a child easy to read, and neither is offered here as a full answer.

It should also be said what the story does not teach. It does not lay down a rule that children die for what their parents do. The law forbids exactly that in Israel's courts (Deuteronomy 24:16), and the prophet Ezekiel says that each person answers for his own sin (Ezekiel 18).

And the book itself holds a surprise. The sons of Korah did not die (26:11). His line lived, and it became part of Israel's worship. Psalms 42 and 84, among others, carry their name. Whatever happened that day, the family of the chief rebel was not left without mercy.

The chapter does not answer every question it raises. A reader may bring Abraham's question to it: “Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” (Genesis 18:25).

A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Moses and Aaron were told to step aside so that judgment could fall, and they fell on their faces and prayed for the people who opposed them. Ask how you pray for people who have turned against you. And ask what you do with the parts of the Bible that frighten you: skip them, explain them away, or bring them to God as questions.

passages.happening:
God tells Moses to have Eleazar, Aaron's son, take the censers out of the fire, ‘because the censers are holy’ (verse 37). They are to be hammered into sheets to cover the altar. “They will serve as a sign to the Israelites” (verse 38).

Eleazar does so. It is to be a reminder ‘that no outsider who is not a descendant of Aaron should approach to offer incense before the LORD’ (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
A censer was a pan for carrying burning coals, on which incense was laid. The 250 censers were bronze. They had been presented before the LORD, and so they counted as holy and could not go back to ordinary use.

So the instruments of the revolt become part of the altar. Every Israelite who brought an offering afterward would see the hammered bronze and remember the day. Israel is given a memorial of its own failure, set in the most visible place in its worship.

The Bible often does this. It does not hide the shameful chapters of its people's story. It builds reminders of them into worship, so that later generations will learn without having to repeat them.
passages.later:
The altar itself was first overlaid with bronze when it was made (Exodus 38:2). The covering made from the censers was an added layer with a story attached.

Paul says of Israel's wilderness years as a whole, “Now these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us” (1 Corinthians 10:11). He is writing to the church.
passages.asks: Israel hammered the record of its failure onto the altar where everyone would see it. Ask what failure in your own story, or your church's, has been hidden when it should have been remembered. And ask what a truthful reminder of it would look like.

passages.t: Between the living and the dead
passages.happening:
“The next day the whole congregation of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron, saying, ‘You have killed the LORD’s people!’” (verse 41).

The cloud covers the tent and the glory of the LORD appears. God says again that he will consume the congregation, and again Moses and Aaron fall facedown (verse 45). A plague has begun.

Moses tells Aaron to take his censer with fire from the altar and incense, and to go quickly and make atonement. “So Aaron took the censer as Moses had ordered and ran into the midst of the assembly” (verse 47).

“He stood between the living and the dead, and the plague was halted” (verse 48). The dead number 14,700 (verse 49).
passages.hearers:
One day has passed. The people saw the earth open. And the next morning they blame Moses and Aaron for the deaths. The chapter does not flatter the crowd any more than it flattered Korah.

Then the story turns. Aaron is an old man, and he runs. He runs toward the plague. He carries a censer, the very thing that had marked the rebels' presumption the day before. In the wrong hands it brought fire. In the hands of the priest God appointed, it brings rescue.

He does not stand at a safe distance. He goes to the line where the dying are and stands on it, between those already dead and those still alive, and the plague stops where he stands.

This is how the chapter answers Korah. He had asked why Aaron should be priest. The answer is given in an act. The priest is the one who runs into the place of judgment for the sake of the people who turned on him the day before.

The story does not end with the punishment of the rebels. It ends with a priest making atonement. That reverses the direction of the whole chapter.

The number of the dead raises the same questions as the other large numbers in the book. The note on 1:20-46 sets out how they are read.
passages.later:
A psalm remembers Moses in the same way at an earlier crisis: he ‘stood before Him in the breach to divert His wrath from destroying them’ (Psalm 106:23).

The New Testament says of Jesus, “Therefore He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them” (Hebrews 7:25). Aaron with his censer is one of the Old Testament's clearest pictures of a mediator. The New Testament draws the pattern out. The story itself is not a hidden prediction.
passages.asks: Aaron ran toward the people who had accused him and stood between them and death. Ask who stands in danger near you, and whether you have kept a safe distance because of how they have treated you. And ask what it would mean to stand in the gap for them, in prayer or in some costlier way.
